section: Early Vedic society and economy - pastoralism, gavishti, varna origins, position of women
subsections: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits
Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: In the early Vedic period, exchange was primarily conducted through which system?
accepted.x: Exchange in the early Vedic period was conducted mainly through barter, as coins had not yet come into use.
accepted.tq: Use the basic economic feature to distinguish barter from later monetary systems.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s: Which of the following was regarded as the standard unit of value and exchange in the early Vedic period?
accepted.x: The cow was the standard unit of value and exchange in the early Vedic economy.
accepted.tq: Identify the standard of value rather than a later monetary unit.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding nishka in the Vedic period:
1. In the Rigveda, it denoted a gold ornament or necklace.
2. In later times, it denoted a unit of value or a gold piece.
3. It was a regularly circulated coin in the Rig Vedic age.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Nishka was a gold ornament in the Rigveda and later came to denote a unit of value or gold piece. It was not a regular coin in the Rig Vedic age.
accepted.tq: Separate the early ornamental meaning of nishka from its later monetary sense.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s: Which one of the following was NOT a unit of value associated with the later use of nishka?
accepted.x: Krishnala, hiranyapinda and mana are listed among the units associated with value in this context. Dinar is not included.
accepted.tq: Find the outsider from a list of closely related units.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s: The Panis of the early Vedic period were primarily associated with which occupation?
accepted.x: The Panis were traders. They were described as wealthy in cattle, greedy and non-Aryan.
accepted.tq: Match the named social group with its principal occupation.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s:
The Panis were condemned in Vedic literature mainly because they were regarded as:
1. Greedy traders
2. Rich in cattle
3. Non-Aryan groups who hid cattle
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The Panis were traders, were associated with cattle wealth, and were condemned as greedy and non-Aryan groups who hid cattle. All three statements are correct.
accepted.tq: Check whether all attributes belong to the same group before selecting the combined option.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s: Which of the following best explains why extensive sea trade is considered doubtful in the Rig Vedic period?
o: The Rigveda prohibits all forms of travel by water.
The term samudra referred only to a river crossing.
The Vedic people used only land routes and had no boats.
Samudra could mean a mass of water, while towns and coinage were absent.
accepted.x: Samudra is understood as a mass of water, but its reference does not establish sea trade. The absence of towns and coinage also indicates limited trade.
accepted.tq: Combine the textual meaning of a term with the economic context instead of making an absolute inference.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s: Wealth in the early Vedic society circulated substantially through which of the following?
accepted.x: Dana referred to gifts, while Dakshina referred to fees or payments made to priests. These were important channels through which wealth circulated.
accepted.tq: Distinguish indigenous forms of redistribution from later fiscal institutions.
accepted.sec: Exchange and ornaments - nishka, barter, Panis, trade limits

accepted.s: The four-fold social classification described in the Purusha Sukta is associated with which Mandala of the Rigveda?
accepted.x: The Purusha Sukta occurs in Mandala X of the Rigveda and is generally regarded as a late addition.
accepted.tq: Use the specific textual location to distinguish the late hymn from earlier Rigvedic material.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the body part mentioned in the Purusha Sukta?
accepted.x: The Purusha Sukta describes Brahmana as originating from the mouth, Kshatriya from the arms, Vaishya from the thighs and Shudra from the feet.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure body-part association and eliminate the reversed pairs.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Purusha Sukta is treated as a late addition to the Rigveda.
2. It describes Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra as emerging from different parts of the cosmic being.
3. It presents the four-fold varna arrangement in its developed form.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements correctly describe the Purusha Sukta and its place in the development of the varna classification.
accepted.tq: Recognise the option containing all mutually consistent features of one hymn.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: The first appearance of the term Shudra is associated with which part of the Rigveda?
accepted.x: The term Shudra first appears in Mandala X of the Rigveda, which contains the Purusha Sukta.
accepted.tq: Test the precise textual location rather than the broader text name alone.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: The distinction between Arya varna and Dasa varna in the early Vedic period primarily reflected a:
o: Cultural and linguistic distinction between groups
Religious division between two priestly orders
accepted.x: Arya and Dasa varna reflected a cultural, linguistic and partly colour-based distinction between Vedic groups and conquered local groups; it was not yet a rigid caste system.
accepted.tq: Distinguish an early cultural distinction from the later birth-based caste structure.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: Which statement best characterises early Vedic society?
o: It was dominated exclusively by a slave-owning aristocracy.
It had a fully developed four-fold caste system in all communities.
It was largely egalitarian, with occupations not fixed by birth.
It was rigidly organised into hereditary occupations from the beginning.
accepted.x: Early Vedic society was largely tribal and egalitarian, and occupations were not rigidly determined by birth.
accepted.tq: Avoid projecting later social institutions onto the earlier period.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: The Vaishya group is described as having developed from which group?
accepted.x: Vaishyas were described as emerging from vis, meaning the mass of the people or tribespeople.
accepted.tq: Match the social category with its stated origin term.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: Which of the following statements regarding slavery in the early Vedic period is correct?
o: Slavery was completely absent from Vedic society.
Slavery formed the principal basis of the entire economy.
Only foreign merchants could be enslaved.
Dasa and Dasyu captives existed, and slave women could be gifted to priests.
accepted.x: Dasa and Dasyu captives and slave women are mentioned, including slave women gifted to priests. However, slavery was not the base of the economy.
accepted.tq: Reject absolute statements and identify the limited but documented presence of slavery.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: Which one of the following illustrates occupational mobility in Rig Vedic society?
o: Craft occupations could be performed only by slaves.
Priestly occupations were prohibited to members of other groups.
All occupations were assigned by birth to members of one varna.
A hymn states that the speaker was a poet, his father a physician and his mother a grinder of corn.
accepted.x: The Rig Vedic hymn describing a poet, a physician father and a mother who ground corn illustrates that occupation was not strictly birth-bound.
accepted.tq: Use a concrete textual example to infer the broader social principle.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: Which of the following features was absent from early Rig Vedic society?
o: Broad social groups of priests, warriors and common people
accepted.x: Untouchability and gotra organisation were absent in the early Rig Vedic society. Slavery and occupational diversity were present.
accepted.tq: Identify the institution that belongs to a later phase rather than the early period.
accepted.sec: Varna origins - Purusha Sukta, first use of 'varna', arya/dasa

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly describes the family structure of the early Vedic period?
o: Egalitarian household without a recognised head
accepted.x: The early Vedic family was patriarchal, patrilineal and generally joint in structure.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the three connected features of household organisation.
accepted.sec: Family - patriarchy, kula, grihapati

accepted.s: The head of the early Vedic household was known as the:
accepted.x: The head of the family was called Grihapati or Kulapa. Gramani, Vispati and Rajan were associated with larger social units.
accepted.tq: Separate household titles from titles belonging to village, clan or tribal levels.
accepted.sec: Family - patriarchy, kula, grihapati

accepted.s: In the early Vedic family, the wife was referred to as:
accepted.x: Sapatni was the term used for the wife in the early Vedic family context.
accepted.tq: Test the exact kinship term rather than a similar occupational title.
accepted.sec: Family - patriarchy, kula, grihapati

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
accepted.x: Kula means family, Grama village, Vis clan and Jana tribe. Therefore, Vis—clan is correctly matched.
accepted.tq: Use the hierarchy to distinguish neighbouring social units with similar labels.
accepted.sec: Family - patriarchy, kula, grihapati

accepted.s: Which statement regarding gotra in the Vedic period is correct?
o: Gotra was identical with kula in the Rigveda.
Gotra referred exclusively to a craft guild.
Gotra was first named in the Atharvaveda, and gotra exogamy developed later.
Gotra was fully developed in the Rigveda and regulated marriage from the beginning.
accepted.x: Gotra is absent in the Rigveda, is first named in the Atharvaveda, and gotra exogamy is a Later Vedic development.
accepted.tq: Separate early Rig Vedic institutions from Later Vedic developments.
accepted.sec: Family - patriarchy, kula, grihapati

accepted.s: Which of the following statements about the terms Jana and Janapada is correct?
o: Janapada is mentioned 275 times, while Jana is absent.
Jana is mentioned 275 times, whereas Janapada is not mentioned.
Jana referred to a village and Janapada to a family.
Both terms are mentioned equally often in the Rigveda.
accepted.x: Jana is mentioned 275 times in the Rigveda, while the term Janapada does not occur there.
accepted.tq: Use the exact frequency and textual absence to eliminate reversed claims.
accepted.sec: Family - patriarchy, kula, grihapati

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Craftsman)
A. Takshan
B. Karmara
C. Hiranyakara
D. Bhishak

List-II (Work)
1. Physician
2. Carpenter
3. Goldsmith
4. Metal smelter or smith

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
accepted.x: Takshan was a carpenter, Karmara a metal worker, Hiranyakara a goldsmith and Bhishak a physician.
accepted.tq: Start from the certain pair and verify the remaining occupational matches.
accepted.sec: Occupations and crafts

accepted.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
accepted.x: Charmamna referred to a tanner, while Bhishak was the physician. The other pairs are correctly matched.
accepted.tq: Look for the swapped occupational title in a list of craft terms.
accepted.sec: Occupations and crafts

accepted.s: In the Rig Vedic context, the term ayas referred to:
accepted.x: Ayas in the Rigveda referred to copper or bronze. Iron was designated as krishna ayas in a later context.
accepted.tq: Distinguish the early meaning of ayas from the later expression for iron.
accepted.sec: Occupations and crafts

accepted.s: Which of the following statements regarding crafts and transport in the early Vedic period is correct?
o: Weaving was unknown and boats were not used.
Weaving was known, was largely undertaken by women, and transport included carts, chariots and boats.
Only iron tools were used in all crafts.
Transport was restricted to elephants and pack horses.
accepted.x: Weaving was known, with women undertaking much of it. Transport included bullock carts, chariots called ratha and boats called nau.
accepted.tq: Combine the correct craft and transport features while rejecting absolute exclusions.
accepted.sec: Occupations and crafts

accepted.s: Which term denoted a weaver in the early Vedic period?
accepted.x: Vaya was the term associated with a weaver. Bhishak meant physician, while Kulapa and Gramani were social titles.
accepted.tq: Distinguish a craft term from household and administrative titles.
accepted.sec: Occupations and crafts

accepted.s: The sacred drink Soma was prepared from a plant believed to have been brought from the:
accepted.x: The Soma plant was associated with the Mujavant mountains and was used to prepare the sacred drink Soma.
accepted.tq: Test the precise geographical association of a ritual substance.
accepted.sec: Food, drink and pastimes

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Soma and sura?
o: Soma was a sacred drink from a plant, while sura was an intoxicating drink.
Sura was a ritual fee paid to priests, while Soma was a unit of value.
Soma was an intoxicating drink and sura was a sacred plant.
Both terms referred to varieties of milk.
accepted.x: Soma was the sacred drink prepared from a plant, whereas sura was an intoxicating drink.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between two similar ritual and intoxicating beverages.
accepted.sec: Food, drink and pastimes

accepted.s: Which of the following constituted important food items in the early Vedic period?
o: Milk and milk products, barley preparations and meat on occasions
Rice, tea and sugarcane products exclusively
Fish and imported spices as the staple diet
accepted.x: Milk and milk products, barley preparations and meat on occasions formed part of the early Vedic diet.
accepted.tq: Select the complete diet description without adding later staples.
accepted.sec: Food, drink and pastimes

accepted.s: Which of the following was NOT a recognised pastime of the early Vedic people?
accepted.x: Chariot racing, dicing, music, dance and hunting were recognised pastimes. Coin-operated gambling in urban markets does not belong to this context.
accepted.tq: Identify the activity that depends on an urban monetary setting absent in the period.
accepted.sec: Food, drink and pastimes

accepted.s: The gambler's hymn is found in which portion of the Rigveda?
accepted.x: The gambler's hymn is found in Rigveda X.34 and is associated with the pastime of dicing.
accepted.tq: Use the precise textual reference to identify the relevant hymn.
accepted.sec: Food, drink and pastimes
